title: A Snapshot of Influence: A Local Data Attribution Framework for Online Rei

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims IIF 'completely eliminates sample inefficiency, achieves unprecedented training speed, and solves the long-standing challenge of training instability in online RL.' However, the actual reported results (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 6b) show only a 20–67% reduction in training rounds and runtime, not elimination of sample inefficiency, and no dedicated analysis of training instability (variance across runs) is presented to support 'solves' this long-standing challenge.

The text states 'Our groundbreaking contributions represent a revolutionary breakthrough in RL interpretability and are threefold,' which is excessive self-congratulatory rhetoric unsupported by the modest empirical gains reported (e.g., 20-80% efficiency improvements in narrow benchmark environments).

The paper cites 'Kumar et al. [2024]' twice in the Introduction, claiming it 'demonstrated that data attribution methods can be directly applied to online RL without modification, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.' However, no 'Kumar' entry appears anywhere in the References section, indicating a fabricated or missing citation.

The text first states that Kumar et al. [2024] showed data attribution 'can be directly applied to online RL without modification, achieving state-of-the-art results,' but then immediately claims 'applying data attribution to online RL is non-trivial' and that existing methods 'fail to account for this key effect of data–model dependency.' These two claims directly contradict each other.

f^return(θ) := E[log π_θ(a|s)·(−Â^ref(s,a))] includes a negative sign on the advantage. The text then states 'Maximizing f^return(θ) encourages increasing the probability of better-than-average actions,' but with the negative sign, maximizing f^return for actions with positive advantage would require decreasing log π_θ(a|s), contradicting the stated interpretation. This is also inconsistent with the analogous RLHF target f^seq(θ) = E[log π_θ(y|x)·Â^ref_{-1}(x,y)], which has no negative sign.

Appendix B.7 states: 'Our main experiments in traditional RL environments are conducted using the SGD optimizer (see Appendix A.2).' However, Appendix A.2 explicitly states: 'learning_rate=5e-3 with optimizer=SGD in all environments except BipedalWalker, for which we use 3e-4 with Adam,' meaning the main BipedalWalker experiments already use Adam, contradicting the blanket claim in B.7.

The text states 'total_timesteps per environment are: ... 1,024,000 for BipedalWalker (1000 rounds)' with n_steps=2048. However, 1,024,000 / 2048 = 500, not 1000, which is inconsistent with the stated round count (other environments' round counts, e.g., FrozenLake 102,400/2048=50, match correctly, confirming the BipedalWalker figure is erroneous).

For FrozenLake, standard PPO per-round optimization time is 2.01s over 50 rounds = 100.5s, yet the reported 'Total runtime (All rounds)' for standard PPO is only 93.85s, which is less than the optimization time alone — mathematically impossible since total runtime must include optimization plus additional overhead (sampling, etc.). The same inconsistency appears for Acrobot (2.02s×50=101s vs. reported total 79.87s) and Highway (3.29s×100=329s vs. reported total 233.66s).

predicted_errors.error_location: Fig. 6(b) vs. Appendix Table 2 (Section B.6) and Table 5 (Section B.9)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The main experiments use filtering percentages described as optimal in Appendix B.6 (p=50% for FrozenLake/Acrobot, p=12.5% for MiniGrid/LunarLander). However, Fig. 6(b) SE_ave/SE_peak values (e.g., MiniGrid SE_ave=78.5%, SE_peak=82.3%) differ substantially from Table 2's reported values at the corresponding p (MiniGrid p=12.5%: SE_ave=23.5%, SE_peak=15.6%). Similarly, Fig. 6(b) RT_peak values (e.g., MiniGrid 81.7%) differ from Table 5's RT_peak values (MiniGrid 71.59%). These are substantial, unexplained discrepancies between figures/tables that should report consistent numbers for the same configuration.

The text states 'IIF achieves substantial sample efficiency gains, showing a 20–67% reduction in training rounds required to match the standard training performance across environments,' but Fig. 6(b) reports SE_peak for MiniGrid as 82.3% ± 2.8%, which exceeds the claimed 20-67% range.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix B.6, Table 2 vs. surrounding text
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims 'Discarding all negative records (p = 100%) is suboptimal,' yet Table 2 shows that for MiniGrid, p=100% achieves the highest (bolded, best) SE_ave of 75.4%, directly contradicting this generalization and the subsequent recommendation to use p=12.5% for MiniGrid in main experiments.

The paper recommends filtering percentages p=50% for Highway and p=6.25% for BipedalWalker in the main experiments (Sec. 5.2), but the ablation study in Table 2 (Appendix B.6) only reports results for FrozenLake, Acrobot, MiniGrid, and LunarLander — no ablation data is provided to justify the chosen p values for Highway or BipedalWalker.
